docs.title: split-resolution-a-part
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-11. Status: superseded.

Decision. When several split parts of a postcode are valid, every lookup resolves to the A part by default and reports status a_part. A split="report" rule returns split_consensus or split_conflict instead. The result's label records which rule was used. Python and SQL are tested to agree under both.

Reason. NRS builds the Scottish Statistics Postcode Lookup by converting split postcodes to the A part, because A is the part with more addresses, so every official statistic uses that convention. Matching it by default means an analyst reconciling against official figures gets the same answer; the report rule keeps the ambiguity visible for anyone who wants it. Supersedes the never-choose-A rule of lookup-statuses.

Evidence. NRS Scottish Statistics Postcode Lookup information note; SPD 2026/2 bulletin on suffix ordering; docs/NRS_GUIDANCE_CHECK.md. On the synthetic cohort, 56 events resolve as a_part.

docs.title: split-suffix-derived-from-key
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-20. Status: implemented.

Decision. The NRS split suffix is derived once, as the key minus its base, and every ranking and status reads that: part_of() in core/spd.py for pandas, _part() and _tier() in the SQL generator, and a part column in the walkthrough. The order among candidates is the whole record ranked as A, so whole and A tie and the newest wins between them, then B, then C, then any later suffix in letter order. Only a whole record or an A part supplies values; a B or C part is still refused with split_a_missing. Two deliberate changes follow. The walkthrough now withholds geography for an ambiguous postcode and for a B or C part, as the generated queries always did, so its status and its empty values agree. And when only B and C are live, B is the reported part rather than the pair being called ambiguous, in both the SQL and the build comparison.

Reason. The A-part rule was tested with the last character of pc_norm in six places. That only worked because a whole-record test always ran in front of it: whole postcodes end in A, B and C too, so the test was one reordering away from misreading them as parts. The B-then-C order decides only which part is reported as matched, never which value is used, because neither part may supply one.

Evidence. G71 8BQB is a whole postcode ending in B and resolves as one. NRS introduces and retires the parts together: no date in the SPD 2026/2 directory has a B or C part valid without its A, so nothing on the real table resolves differently, and the rebuilt tables keep their fingerprints. Two agreement cases in tests/test_agreement.py pin the whole postcode ending in B and the B-and-C-only case. Commit 413c024. Column counts quoted in sql-two-products and sql-as-of-address-date, 91, 107 and 110, predate shared-exports, which removed the coordinate columns: the queries now return 89, 103 and 106.

Columns (1): pc_base

docs.title: sql-as-of-address-date
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-13. Status: implemented.

Decision. The SPD set adds link_as_of.sql with input id, postcode, address_date, analysis_year. As a project policy, select lives in [introduced_on, deleted_on), apply the whole/A preference among valid lives, follow a large user's exact link to the small-user life valid on that date, and choose the edition from analysis_year. Report postcode_not_yet_introduced, between_lives or postcode_deleted_by_date when no life contains the date, and missing_address_date for a known key with no date. Return first_introduced_on, previous_life_deleted_on and next_life_introduced_on as context. The 41-column core is shared with the other queries, but the added dates make 110 total columns. SSPL has no dated query because NRS kept one life per postcode.

Reason. Latest-life matching can assign a re-used postcode's new location to an older address: 2,957 reviewed SPD postcodes have a latest life in a different 2011 zone from the life before, 2,030 with a different 2020v2 quintile. A reliable address date can distinguish these lives; a general CHI record edit timestamp must not be assumed to describe residence without checking its meaning. Keep address date separate from the health data year. This policy does not reconstruct historical administrative or rurality snapshots; context remains what the downloaded release supplies for the selected life.

Evidence. FK17 8DS: 1975 resolves to the 1973 life in S01013116 (quintile 5), 1990 to the 1978 life in S01013113 (quintile 3), June 1978 falls between the lives. TD9 7PQ: matched on 15 May 1990 with matched_is_current false, deleted by date on its deletion day, not yet introduced in 1970. tests/test_sql_sets.py covers the interval boundaries, the gap, the split and link rules on a date, and every recorded life on its own introduction day against the built table.

docs.title: sql-as-of-year-from-address-date
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-18. Status: implemented.

Decision. In the dated query analysis_year becomes an override rather than a required input. The requested step now settles it as COALESCE(analysis_year, YEAR(address_date)), so a cohort supplies id, postcode and address_date and the SIMD edition follows the year that date falls in. A non-null analysis_year still wins, unchanged, and the year the query reports is the one it used. missing_year therefore now means neither was given, while a null address date is still reported on its own as missing_address_date. This supersedes the part of sql-as-of-address-date that required both inputs; the life-selection rules are untouched.

Reason. For the usual source the two are one date: an SMR01 episode's admission date is both the address date and the year of the event, so requiring the year twice invited a mismatch without offering anything. Deriving makes the common case right by construction and each row gets the edition current when it happened. Keeping the override preserves the case that motivated separating them, PHS v3.5 section 3.2.1.2, where one classification is held across a long comparison, and the case where the address was recorded at a different time from the health event. It is the same pattern the latest-life queries already use for their single EDIT EDITION line: the default is the ordinary reading and the alternative is explicit.

Evidence. Both the generated query and the hand-written walkthrough were changed together and the equivalence test now carries five rows with a null year among its fifteen cases. On the built SPD table the derived rows report 2015, 2019, 1975, 2005 and 2008 and select SIMD 2016, 2020v2, none, 2006 and 2009v2, the third showing that deriving a year before 1996 leaves no edition, which is where the override earns its place: FK17 8DS on 1 June 1975 with analysis_year 2020 still reads the 1973 life, S01013116, on SIMD 2020v2. The walkthrough's demo carries one row of each kind. tests/test_sql_sets.py covers the default, the override, and both inputs missing at once.

docs.title: sql-latest-linked-postcodes
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: superseded.

Decision. Two SQL examples share one latest-postcode view. One uses a chosen SIMD edition (default 2020v2); one uses PHS v3.5 Table 4 by event year. Both use PHS population-weighted Scotland quintiles, 1 most deprived. The date selects the edition, not a historical postcode life. Ordinary split postcodes use A; large users use the latest record of the exact named small-user link, including an explicit split suffix. Missing/unusable links have null SIMD, never an own-geography fallback. Keep every event row and expose both matched and source natural keys.

Reason. The user chose the linked-small-user route. Keep edition choice separate from postcode selection and put shared rules in one reviewable place. PHS's postcode page describes latest versions and A parts; Appendix A describes large-user links but does not fully specify own-versus-linked disagreement. Exact equivalence to a published PHS postcode lookup remains unverified.

Evidence. docs/LINKAGE_BY_ERA.md maps code to guidance and labels project choices; tests/test_sql.py uses explicit fixtures and downloaded-data checks. SPD 2026/2 example AB11 6GN has own 2020v2 quintile 2 but linked AB11 6BE supplies 3.

docs.title: sql-representative-and-interface-boundary
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: implemented.

Decision. For the SPD SQL setup and the cross-table comparison, select the newest life per full key across both user types, then prefer live records, whole/A, and newest introduction per ordinary postcode. Ties and missing A receive no geography. Retain last-known deleted records, including named small-user link targets, with current flags. Missing dates and years without an edition have distinct statuses. Accept ordinary input postcodes only. SSPL already selects latest whole records upstream. Python keeps its separate current/as-of, own-record geography policy; no Python/SQL parity is claimed.

Reason. This ordering and complete deleted-record retention are explicit project policies, not a claim to reproduce PHS's unpublished selection details. Do not silently change existing Python consumers or revive an older small-user record when the newest life is an unlinked large user. New SIMD editions and year mappings require separate review.

docs.title: sql-review-corrections
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-13. Status: implemented.

Decision. Correct SQL Server bit predicates to is_current = 1. Resolve dated lookups per distinct normalised postcode/address-date pair and join back to original inputs, without an execution-dependent row number; preserve duplicates and null IDs. Test output mappings independently of the generator, including a deliberately swapped quintile/decile regression, every stored edition, selected geographies and own-record context. Clarify the preceding decisions' output contracts and guidance claims without changing postcode linkage policy, source pins or stored data values.

Reason. SQL Server requires a predicate for bit fields and does not materialise CTEs; unordered ROW_NUMBER values are not stable join keys across references. A shared production/test mapping can hide column swaps. Reviewers must distinguish documented guidance, project interpretations and native runtime verification that remains outstanding.

Evidence. Microsoft Learn: bit (Transact-SQL), CASE (Transact-SQL), WITH common_table_expression (Transact-SQL), ROW_NUMBER (Transact-SQL). tests/test_sql_sets.py exercises generated queries in DuckDB; these checks do not establish SQL Server runtime compatibility.

docs.title: sql-two-products-no-default
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-13. Status: implemented.

Decision. Two SQL sets, docs/sql/spd reading postcode_simd_history (key pc_norm, introduced_on) and docs/sql/sspl reading postcode_simd (key pc_norm), with no default or cross-product fallback. Each has standalone link_by_era.sql (id, postcode, analysis_year; edition by PHS v3.5 Table 4) and link_latest.sql (id, postcode; one edition throughout), with numbered steps distinguishing guidance from project choices. They share a 41-column core through band_direction, then append different own-record context: SSPL has 91 columns, SPD era/latest 107. Select common columns by name when combining results. The SPD set selects the latest life per full NRS key, then prefers live, whole or A, newest introduction; a best B/C-only record gets split_a_missing, a tie gets ambiguous_postcode, both without SIMD. SSPL needs neither selection step. Both follow LinkedSmallUserPostcode to a small-user record: SPD uses the exact suffix; SSPL accepts an A alias only for a whole record flagged SplitIndicator Y, and cannot resolve B/C. NO LINKP gets po_box, NO LINK/blank/null gets unlinked_large_user, without SIMD. The source record supplies all 14 stored measures and selected-vintage geographies; the matched record's own fields remain context. No chaining through large users.

Reason. Product and edition policy remain explicit study choices, but NRS recommends SSPL for statistical production and SPD for operational/administrative use. Applying linked-small-user geography to SSPL is a project interpretation of PHS Appendix A, which describes links and absent geography for PO boxes/unlinked large users but does not explicitly settle overriding geography already allocated in SSPL. Absence of contrary NRS guidance is not endorsement. Preserve the chosen policy pending authoritative confirmation or comparison with a PHS postcode-level oracle; retaining own-record context makes its effect visible. The SSPL suffix rule is also a project interpretation. Exact PHS lookup parity remains unverified.

Evidence. PHS v3.5 Appendix A pp.28-30, Table 4 p.17, sections 3.1-3.4; PHS postcode-file page (most recent version, A part only); NRS SSPL information note and 2026/2 dictionary; NRS SPD 2026/2 dictionary on PO-box grid references. Worked example AB24 2TY: own 2020v2 quintile 5, linked AB24 2TN quintile 1, identical in both tables. Plan: docs/plans/SQL_Two_Products_Plan.md.

docs.title: sspl-allocation-is-part-of-the-contract
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: implemented.

Decision. The main table's data zones are the SSPL's: every higher geography is the one containing the centroid of the postcode's 2022 output area. The history table's data zones are the SPD's: the zone containing the postcode's own grid reference. Each table's metadata names its method (allocation: oa2022_centroid or postcode_grid_reference), the data dictionary states it, and every build reports how many current postcodes differ between the two tables and how many SIMD bands change as a result. The difference is an observation, never a gate, and never reconciled by editing either table.

Reason. A user must be able to see which allocation method a table follows. The comparison reports observed differences, not a causal decomposition into release and allocation effects. It compares own-record bands before linked-small-user selection. Neither shared inputs nor matching bands establish equivalence to a PHS postcode-level lookup.

Evidence. NRS information note and current build report. The preliminary SSPL 2026/1 comparison in the historical plan used different PAF cuts and incorrect representatives for 19 postcodes; its provisional counts and cause claims are not acceptance evidence.

docs.title: sspl-direct-sql-both-publishers
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-13. Status: superseded.

Decision. Default SQL takes postcode and integer analysis year. Use the exact matched SSPL record's geography, never redirect large users or resolve splits again. Map the year to SIMD using PHS v3.5 Table 4 and return all 14 ingested PHS/Government measures, distinctly labelled, with the selected data-zone vintage and PHS local-band geography codes. Keep every input row and report postcode/year/missing-value statuses independently of address warnings. PO boxes, unlinked large users and deleted records retain source values; residence eligibility and publication choices are downstream. Preserve the earlier SPD linked-small-user examples under docs/sql/history, not as a default fallback.

Reason. The user chose SSPL's published allocation and requested both publishers so later analysis can choose measures. Re-following links overrides that allocation: in SSPL 2026/2 it changed 147 PHS 2020v2 quintiles, including 50 live postcodes. NRS supplies postcode geography; PHS supplies the health-year edition policy and population-weighted bands. This is not a claim of exact PHS postcode-lookup equivalence or a pre-filtered residential cohort.

Evidence. NRS SSPL information note; PHS v3.5 sections 3.1-3.4, Table 4 and Appendix A. tests/test_sql_sspl.py checks every reshaped value and PHS geography across the saved editions, all year boundaries, duplicate/unmatched events, and unchanged large-user own values. AB24 2TY retains quintile 5, rather than linked AB24 2TN's quintile 1. SQL Server runtime verification remains separate.

docs.title: sspl-main-table
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: implemented.

Decision. Two tables from two NRS products. The main table, postcode_simd.parquet, is built from the Scottish Statistics Postcode Lookup (SSPL): one row per whole postcode, both user types, latest life including deleted postcodes, key pc_norm. The history table, postcode_simd_history.parquet, is the existing SPD build: every postcode life, key (pc_norm, introduced_on), rows unchanged. Neither table is derived from the other.

Reason. NRS recommends SSPL for statistical production. History is still needed for date-valid postcode matching and inspecting split parts. Choosing an SIMD edition by event year does not itself require postcode history: the default SQL era query reads SSPL.

Evidence. docs/plans/SSPL_Main_Table_Plan.md section 1: SSPL 2026/1 has 229,708 unique whole postcodes, both data-zone vintages, no blank geography, PO-box sentinels, and deletion dates.

docs.title: sspl-migration-review
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-13. Status: superseded.

Decision. Version 2.0.1 reconciles the migration. Pin SSPL 2026/2 (230103 rows, 161822 live, 187490 small users, 42613 large users); update the two Scottish Parliament columns to 2026 and main schema to postcode_simd_sspl_v2. Default SQL reads main; create_latest_postcode_lookup_history.sql is the explicit SPD alternative. Both share the two edition queries and return index_source, index_release, allocation and requested_link_postcode. SSPL accepts a linked A suffix only for a flagged small-user split representative; B/C cannot resolve. Never fall back across products. Correct the comparison selection and remove unsupported causal/PHS-parity claims.

Reason. The implementation, decision log and examples must agree. Preserve the SPD history fingerprint independently of an SSPL refresh, and check the new main fingerprint only against its own reviewed source pins and schema. Keep historical plans clearly superseded.

Evidence. tests/test_agreement.py checks synthetic and real SQL parity; tests/test_sql_sspl.py covers SSPL-only links, exclusions, era boundaries and row preservation; build/audit read back both saved tables against pinned sources. Original SSPL 2026/1 archive hash b8bc805567a167dd23a8891dddf44855a8174ddff3885c7f3caa0defc8d83478 and row fingerprint 6c14f4596b3fabb2c814d0af945eae02e00ea330f7440791437990ef4d98aa0f are retained as historical evidence.

docs.title: sspl-totals-are-counted-not-published
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: implemented.

Decision. NRS publishes no record counts for the SSPL. The registry pins the counted totals of the pinned file (all, live, small user, large user) and marks them counted. They are blocking gates like the SPD's published totals, because they detect a changed or truncated file, but they are not independent evidence from the publisher.

Reason. The pipeline's rule is that a count gate is an input a reviewer can check against something outside the build. For the SSPL the only external check is the file hash, so the totals must be labelled for what they are.

Evidence. SSPL 2026/1 bulletin and data dictionary carry no totals. Counted: 229,708 all; 161,565 live; 187,173 small user; 42,535 large user.

docs.title: trust-the-sources
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-11. Status: implemented.

Decision. No SIMD value is recomputed or compared between publishers. The population reconstruction diagnostic, the band-formula checks and the PHS-versus-government divergence fingerprints are removed. The one remaining cross-source check is that PHS and the Scottish Government list the same data zones with the same ranks in every edition.

Reason. The pipeline's guarantee is that the published values reach the table unchanged, which the hash pins, the per-step checks and the readback establish. Recomputing bands to see whether the publisher's method can be reproduced answered a different question and made the build harder to read. The rank check stays because it is what justifies joining the two sources on the data zone.

Evidence. Removing these checks changes no value; the output remains byte-identical.

Columns (6): simd2004_rank, simd2006_rank, simd2009v2_rank, simd2012_rank, simd2016_rank, simd2020v2_rank

docs.title: two-nrs-cuts
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: implemented.

Decision. The SSPL and the SPD pinned together need not be the same PAF cut; each table records its own release label. Cross-table differences in postcode presence, introduction date, live status and user type are reported as observations. A pin is chosen by hand for each product.

Reason. The products may be refreshed independently, but there is no need to retain an older SSPL when the intended newer release is available. The current pins are both 2026/2. Matching release labels still do not establish the cause of each geography difference.

Evidence. SSPL 2026/2 publication, 18 August 2026, July PAF: https://www.nrscotland.gov.uk/publications/scottish-statistics-postcode-lookup-20262/. The older SSPL 2026/1 pin was superseded by sspl-migration-review.

docs.title: visible-steps-and-build-report
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-11. Status: superseded.

Decision. The build is written as small named steps in code: one function per directory file, per PHS file as published, per canonicalised PHS edition, per government edition, and one join per edition, each with its own checks. The Dagster graph stays at five things, sources plus four tables, and the steps appear as rows in a build report, results/BUILD_REPORT.md, written by every build in plain language with that run's numbers. docs/HOW_IT_IS_BUILT.md is the static one-page companion.

Reason. A first attempt exposed every step as a graph node, fifty-one in all, and a reviewer could not read it. A graph is a machine's view; a reviewer needs a narrative with numbers. The steps stay visible where they help, in the code and the report, and out of the graph where they do not.

Evidence. CLI and Dagster builds on branch ladder both produced sha256 c685cd137652ec37 under main's decision log, byte-identical to main. Twenty-two assets, twenty-four checks, intermediates about 16 MB of Parquet.

docs.title: walkthrough-both-bandings-and-rurality
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-18. Status: implemented.

Decision. The walkthrough returns the Scottish Government unweighted quintile and decile beside the PHS population-weighted ones, and the 6-fold and 8-fold urban-rural codes with a label for the 6-fold. The unweighted bands come from the record that supplied the data zone; the rurality comes from the matched record itself, which is what the generated query does, so a large user reports its own point location rather than that of the small-user postcode it links to. Its demo input became three rows, and the equivalence test now compares these four columns too.

Reason. A reader validating the logic has to see that the same rank produces two different bands: PHS splits so each band holds a fifth or a tenth of the population, the Scottish Government splits the data zones themselves, and a report that mixes them is wrong in a way nothing else catches. Rurality is routinely crossed with deprivation, and holding it next to the band makes its one limitation visible: the directory carries a single 2022 classification, so a historical address is described by today's categories even though its data zone and SIMD are read at the right vintage.

Evidence. Of 162,049 current postcodes with a 2020v2 band, 5,615 fall in a different quintile and 12,216 in a different decile under the two bandings. The demo's second row, AB21 0SB on 1 June 2015, is quintile 3 weighted by population and 4 by data zone, decile 6 against 7. The 6-fold labels are the Scottish Government classification and nest exactly as the two columns do in the data: code 4 covers 8-fold 4 and 5, code 5 covers 6, code 6 covers 7 and 8. The NRS dictionary documents only the ranges, 1 to 6 and 1 to 8.

docs.title: which-table-answers-which-question
docs.text:
Date: 2026-09-12. Status: implemented.

Decision. Python date-valid lookups (on=, attach with a date column, attach_by_era) and split-report requests need SPD history and are refused against SSPL. Default SQL uses own-record SSPL geography and an analysis year to select the edition, returning both publishers and address warnings. Legacy SPD SQL is isolated under docs/sql/history. Python remains current-only/as-of with own-record geography and sentinel exclusion. Both stored tables retain source values for PO boxes and unlinked large users; consumers apply their documented exclusions.

Reason. One latest life per postcode cannot say whether a postcode existed at a date or which zone it was in then. Making the refusal explicit prevents a silent wrong answer. The split and PO-box defaults are unchanged so existing consumers see the same policy.

Evidence. SSPL dictionary: no small-user split postcodes; A part used; counts added. SSPL 2026/1 links: NO LINKP on 27,162 large users, NO LINK on 5, 15,368 real links of which 9 keep an A suffix.
